scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Kapa haka evolved from pre-European Māori performing arts, including haka, mau rākau, poi, and mōteatea.
The modern concert group format emerged in the 1860s, and the national Te Matatini competition has been held since 1972.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Kapa haka is used to express heritage, cultural identity, and community mana.
It is performed at social, official, and competitive events.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Dance Party! 💃 Ballet, Kapa Haka, Jazz And Hip Hop For Kids (https://archive.org/details/dance-party-ballet-kapa-haka-jazz-and-hip-hop-for-kids)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Performances are highly synchronized, involving choral singing and specific movements.
Key techniques include wiri (hand trembling), takahi (foot stamping), and pūkana (eye widening).
Women often perform poi, while men lead the haka.
Watch for Wiri, Pūkana.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is primarily vocal, often featuring European-style harmony and guitar accompaniment.
Traditional instruments include the pūtatara (conch shell), poi, and rākau (sticks).
Listen for the Guitar, Pūtatara, Poi, Rākau.
The pulse is Triple meter (haka).
A blend of European-style vocal harmony and traditional Māori chanting, punctuated by the percussive sounds of poi striking hands and rhythmic foot stamping.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Apirana Ngata is noted for his role in revitalizing Māori culture and developing the waiata-ā-ringa in the early 20th century.
Te Matatini is the national competition, while regional competitions occur across New Zealand and Australia.
The tradition descends from pre-colonial Māori performing arts, incorporating both indigenous forms and European musical influences.
